Photograph: Jeremy Davidson/Getty Images/iStockphoto US news Drone footage shows rare bird’s-eye view of stingrays off New York coast With wing spans up to 3ft, the shy cownose ray species typically arrive in Long Island waters in the warmer months Maya Yang in New York Wed 12 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Drone footage of dozens of stingrays in the ocean off New York has captivated beachgoers and marine enthusiasts, offering a rare bird’s-eye view of a species that scientists say has visited the area for decades. The footage was captured last Friday off the coast of Southampton on the Long Island peninsula by Joanna Steidle, a Hamptons-based professional drone pilot known for her aerial ocean shots . It shows cownose rays gliding through the water en masse near the surface. Describing the rays in a separate drone shot last week, Steidle said on Instagram: “While filming these I can feel my heartbeat and breathing align with their wings flapping....it is in these moments I feel completely connected and present.” The sighting raises the possibility that the species is migrating farther north and appearing in the area more consistently as ocean temperatures rise, or could simply indicate that increased drone use is making everyday wildlife activity more visible to the public, various experts said. Thousands of migrating stingrays spotted off New York coast The video appears to show hundreds of cownose rays swimming in a group that some refer to by the collective noun “fever”, as in a fever of rays. The species is a large, migratory elasmobranch , a subclass of cartilaginous fish, named for their distinctive high-lobed head resembling a cow’s nose. With wing spans stretching up to 3ft (1 meter), the shy and non-aggressive cownose ray feeds mostly on bivalves, including clams and other bottom-dwelling prey. The rays typically arrive in Long Island waters in the warmer months, following water temperatures that suit them as they migrate north from the Chesapeake Bay, the mid-Atlantic estuary, and other waters farther south. As ocean temperatures rise rapidly around the world, driven largely by climate change , scientists say, warmer waters could be contributing to changes in the timing and range of the rays’ migration. Speaking about the sighting, Dean Grubbs, associate director of research at Florida State University’s coastal and marine laboratory, said: “This occurrence probably does represent a northern shift in the migration due to temperature. Historically, there would be some cownose rays that would make it up to Cape Cod or so in small numbers during warm years, but the big schools would terminate the northern migration around Chesapeake Bay. Now, as ocean temperatures warm, the northern migrations of a lot of species are shifting further and further north.” Grubbs pointed to blacktip sharks as a precedent for a northward shift. While that species was rarely seen north of North Carolina in the 1970s, he said, it had become common in Virginia and Delaware by the 1990s and is now frequently found in New England during warm summers. Ryan Wallace, an assistant professor of environmental studies and sciences at Adelphi University, said cownose rays generally prefer water temperatures 70-79F (approximately 21-26C), meaning New York’s warm, coastal waters could drive them to migrate north earlier in the spring and remain in the region longer. “Water temperature kind of dictates that timing, and so that can then trigger – as the drone footage had captured – these large fevers, which can be hundreds, even thousands in some cases,” Wallace said. Cownose rays, however, are not new to Long Island. “The cownose rays are very common, often in very large groups, along beaches of Long Island, New York and Long Beach Island, New Jersey, in the surf and also in the quiet bay waters behind the barrier islands for at least the last 25 years,” said Thomas Grothues, associate research professor at Rutgers University, in New Jersey. “They are ‘newly’ discovered by beachgoers every year and are frequently mistaken for sharks because their wingtips protrude,.” Matthew Ajemian, associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, said cownose rays have been documented in New York’s waters since the 1800s. While there may be more public sightings, he said, researchers must also consider how advances in drone technology have changed the way wildlife is observed by the general public and experts alike. “People are seeing them, I think, more frequently [in real life and online]. We also have to be aware of our observer bias too, because it’s so much easier for us to capture these types of things [nowadays],” Ajemian said, adding: “We have drone technology, which really helps with some of the capacity to see things that are relatively rare, although I guess the correct term for its abundance within New York is ‘uncommon’.” Echoing Ajemian, Kevin Weng, an associate professor at College of William & Mary Virginia Institute of Marine Science, said drones are particularly valuable for observing cownose rays from above, but researchers need to account for where and how often those observations are made. “Drones, amazing. What we need to understand is the distribution of observation effort,” he said. Still, researchers say drones offer a valuable new tool for studying cownose rays, especially when it comes to estimating their size and movement. “Drones are definitely giving us views and a perspective we haven’t seen before for a lot of species. Estimating population abundances for cownose rays is particularly difficult because they travel in such large schools. I think aerial drones may be a useful tool for estimating abundances of species like cownose rays that do spend a substantial amount of time near the surface,” Grubbs said. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9v9.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Volodymyr Zelensky says "the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous" By Harry Sekulich Published 2 September 2026, 05:23 BST Updated 4 hours ago Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes. "We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine has since formally notified the UN of the risks to civilian aviation. Russian President Vladimir Putin said the comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism". Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia because of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries like Turkey and China do. Explaining the elevated airspace risk in his nightly video address on Tuesday, Zelensky said that "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft" and did not want the loss of innocent lives. "There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said. Zelensky directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow. In a statement on X, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Ukraine had officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was not safe for civilian aviation. "We want to prevent unintended incidents," he said, adding: "The war is returning home to Russia." On Wednesday afternoon, flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed many planes flying over Russia, including arriving and departing from the two main airports, which had some delays, but few cancellations. Several airlines that fly through Russia told the BBC that they were carefully monitoring the situation. Qatar Airways, which flies into Moscow and travels through Russian airspace to get to the US west coast, said its flight planning was "guided by rigorous and continuous monitoring of airspace security, safety assessments, and geopolitical developments". Turkish low-cost airline Pegasus cancelled its flights to Russia on Tuesday and Wednesday, citing "technical and operational reasons", but said future flights "are operating as scheduled". FlyDubai, an Emirati government-owned carrier, told the BBC that it would "closely monitor the evolving situation in the region and adjust our flight schedules and routings as necessary". Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West Published 8 hours ago Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory and there have been repeated attacks on depots belonging to Russia's two biggest online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Its drone attacks have for months led to disruption at some of Russia's biggest airports, especially in Moscow where at times all four major airports have been forced to halt arrivals and departures. Several cancellations were reported on Wednesday. Ukraine does not have to target airports to cause disruption. Under Russia's air defence "Kovyor" (carpet) plan, flights are suspended if a drone is detected in the relevant area. Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year. "There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict." Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists." His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Tuesday and further attacks on Odesa, Sumy and Kyiv on Wednesday. Russia's military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations. The Ukrainian capital and its surrounding region have come under attack for seven days in a row. A few weeks ago, Zelensky said Russia was attacking Ukraine every day, and Ukraine's military had "begun the process of bringing the war back to Russia". At the weekend he said the same, that Russia had to feel the war was "returning to where it came from". Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair. Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe. Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022. Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft throughout that period. The risks of civil aviation during a war are clear. A few months after war broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014 between Russian-backed separatists and the Ukrainian military, a Russian-made missile brought down a passenger plane, killing all 298 people on board. Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014. The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster. In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed. He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Photograph: Andrii Tsynhariuk/Alamy View image in fullscreen The Patarkatsishvili family own a 34% stake in one of Ukraine’s main producers of bottled mineral water. Photograph: Andrii Tsynhariuk/Alamy Ukraine Ukraine seeks to seize water company owned by billionaire family of British theatre mogul Dispute centres on stake held by Patarkatsishvili family in bottled water firm it jointly owns with Russian oligarch Daniel Boffey Chief reporter Mon 7 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 04.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British theatre impresario and her billionaire family are embroiled in a bitter dispute with Ukrainian authorities seeking to seize a water company they jointly own with a Russian oligarch. The row centres on a 34% stake held in the producer of Ukraine’s biggest bottled water brands by the Patarkatsishvili family, including Liana Patarkatsishvili, who recently worked on an immersive show with Toby Jones and Meera Syal. The corporate holdings of IDS Ukraine were frozen by the Ukrainian authorities in 2022 owing to the 49% stake that is also held in the company by Russian investors, including Mikhail Fridman, the founder of the Russian Alfa Group conglomerate. He is under western sanctions for his support for Vladimir Putin’s regime. Ukraine’s asset recovery and management agency (Arma) has been tasked with instructing independent management to take over the running of the company whose other minority shareholders include the Georgian government. The Ukrainian agency’s head, Yaroslava Maksymenko, said they had repeatedly run into legal and bureaucratic obstacles owing, in part, to the shareholders’ resistance to give up control of their assets. The agency further claims to have been the subject of a cyber-attack during one attempt to find an independent manager for the company although there is no evidence as to who was responsible and the Patarkatsishvili family is not suspected. However, Maksymenko claimed New World Value Fund Limited, the vehicle for the Patarkatsishvili’s investment in IDS Ukraine, had pursued an unfounded claim of unlawful conduct by Arma’s officials which she said was “misinformation”. An investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine into the claims of unlawful conduct continues. Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’ Read more Maksymenko said her agency had concerns over potential money laundering and value extraction from IDS Ukraine if it remained under the current management although there have not been any official findings of such criminality. There are separate proceedings in the Ukrainian anti-corruption high court in which the shareholders are fighting attempts to nationalise part or all of the ownership of IDS Ukraine, which is seen by some in government as a key strategic asset at a time of war. A spokesperson for the Patarkatsishvili family said they had been committed supporters of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022 , adding that the family were being unfairly targeted and would seek justice in the international courts if necessary. They said: “The Patarkatsishvili family strongly believes that an asset should not be taken away from non-sanctioned shareholders against whom there are no allegations or concerns, and is defending this position through all relevant proceedings before the Ukrainian courts and authorities. “If the Patarkatsishvili family is unable to obtain justice through the Ukrainian courts, and the asset is ultimately taken away through the Arma process, it will, of course, have no choice but to seek justice before the international courts, as it has consistently done in the past.” The family’s shareholding in IDS Ukraine was inherited in 2008 by Liana, her sister, Iya, and mother, Inna, after the death of Badri Patarkatsishvili , a businessman who made his fortune during the breakup of the Soviet Union. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Badri Patarkatsishvili, seen here in 2005, reportedly left behind a £6bn fortune when he died. Photograph: STR New/Reuters Patarkatsishvili fled to the UK in 2007 but died in 2008 of a heart attack at the age of 52 with an estimated fortune of £6bn. Iya Patarkatsishvili and her husband made headlines last year for being granted a refund after buying a £32m London mansion that was said to be infested with moths. Last summer, Liana Patarkatsishvili staged a large-scale immersive theatre production called Storehouse about “misinformation” through her production company Sage & Jester, starring the actors Toby Jones and Meera Syal. A spokesperson for IDS Ukraine said: “Throughout its operations, the IDS Ukraine Group of companies has operated and continues to operate in accordance with the requirements of Ukrainian law, including tax and financial legislation. “No competent state authority of Ukraine, including the state tax service of Ukraine, has established any facts of money laundering, unlawful withdrawal of funds or any other financial activity of this nature on the part of IDS Ukraine. “We are not aware of any investigations or other current inquires of Ukrainian authorities into the operations of IDS Ukraine with respect to any such allegations. “IDS Ukraine has also not ceased operations for a single day since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The group continued production and supplied Ukrainian consumers with drinking water even amid continuous missile and drone attacks.” The spokesperson added: “We are aware of statements by the asset recovery and management agency implying but not saying it directly that [a cyber-attack] is somehow connected with the IDS Ukraine Group of companies. However, this information is simply false and in reality completely irrelevant.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Europe Russia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

During the visit, Trump offered to send more US troops to Poland [FILE: September 3, 2025] Image: Aaron Schwartz/UPI Photo/IMAGO Advertisement US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that significant progress had been made toward establishing a US military base in Poland . "Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. In August, Warsaw revealed that it was in talks with Washington regarding a permanent US military presence in Poland. "If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance," Trump added in a social media post. His announcement comes despite his administration's launch of a formal review of its military presence in Europe. This has raised fears among allies that the US could reduce its military presence there. How did Warsaw react? Nawrocki, who is a conservative ally of the US president, thanked Trump on X, saying Poland was "ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation." He added, "I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base." Meanwhile, Zbigniew Bogucki, the head of the Polish president's chancellery, called Trump's announcement "great news for Poland." He also noted that it came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland. In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said his country was discussing with the United States the possibility of establishing a permanent US base on its territory. "We have already completed the initial stage of the process, not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told the public broadcaster TVP. Can Poland hold NATO’s line against Russia without the US? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Poland secures NATO's eastern flank Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been pushing for a larger allied presence on NATO 's eastern flank. Nearly 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland, a member of both NATO and the EU. However, they are there almost exclusively on a rotational basis. Poland's proximity to Ukraine and Russia is a key factor in its security strategy. The country allocates approximately 5% of its gross domestic product to defense spending and has been working to increase the United States' military presence . In the meantime, Washington heavily criticized several European countries for refusing to allow US forces to use NATO bases in its war with Iran. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Aili Wang was arrested at LAX airport as she allegedly sough to return to China. Photograph: Mark Gomelsky/AP View image in fullscreen Aili Wang was arrested at LAX airport as she allegedly sough to return to China. Photograph: Mark Gomelsky/AP Wyoming Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege Associated Press Tue 13 Oct 2026 20.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her. Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China . With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China. Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea. US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities. The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover. “It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.” Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages. The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie. Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said. Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit. The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said. He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away. Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide. Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine. It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only. Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.
